classifications.label: Systematic calibration error: each instrument has drifted from its true baseline, or baseline was not properly zeroed on Day 1, causing each stream to measure a different offset of the same underlying signal

Environmental or instrumental coupling: the four measurement streams are not independent; they respond to a common disturbance (temperature, vibration, electromagnetic interference) in delayed, phase-inverted, or damped ways, creating the observed offset-dependent anti-correlations and near-zero correlations

Measurement technique or observer bias: the two 'lab' instruments (pendulum_lab, resonator_lab) and the two 'observational' instruments (pendulum_obs, resonator_obs) are not measuring the same physical quantity, or observers are biasing their readings in a way that decorrelates the streams
Residual instrumental noise dominates signal; instruments are functioning but have insufficient signal-to-noise ratio, and observed correlations are largely chance fluctuations within noise floors
Static calibration baseline error on one or more instruments from Day 1
Instrumental or environmental coupling with delayed/damped or phase-inverted response

Environmental or instrumental coupling with thermal/mechanical time constant: lab instruments respond to a common disturbance (vibration, temperature drift, electromagnetic noise) with phase opposition between pendulum and resonator channels; Day 23 spike reflects an acute increase in disturbance amplitude or bandwidth on that day.
Unrecorded procedural change, recalibration, or measurement technique shift affecting lab instruments on Day 12–13 or Day 22–23, introducing increased variance that persists.

Pure instrumental noise and statistical chance: all four streams are independent noise floors, correlations are flukes, and Day 23 variance spike is a random outlier.

Environmental or instrumental coupling: lab instruments respond to a common localized disturbance (thermal, mechanical, or electromagnetic) with phase-dependent inversions; Day 23 reflects acute increase in disturbance amplitude; observational instruments are physically isolated or use passive sensing.

Unrecorded procedural change or recalibration in lab instruments around Day 12–13 or Day 22–23: altered sampling rate, timing, averaging window, observer handling, or equipment adjustment; lab instruments more sensitive to procedural shifts than observational instruments.

All four streams are independent noise floors; observed correlations are statistical flukes; Day 23 variance spike is a random outlier.

Localized environmental or instrumental coupling in lab: lab instruments respond to a common transient disturbance (thermal, mechanical, electromagnetic, or power quality event) on Day 22–23 with damped response; observational instruments physically isolated or use passive sensing insensitive to this disturbance.

Procedural or calibration change in lab instruments between Day 12–23 (most likely Day 22–23): altered sampling rate, averaging window, observer handling, timing, or equipment recalibration affecting only active lab measurement apparatus.

Acute instrumental malfunction or transient physical disturbance (vibration, power surge, RF interference, resonance excitation) in lab on Day 22–23, increasing high-frequency noise in lab instruments without shifting their means; observational instruments unaffected due to isolation or passive design.

Baseline calibration error or instrument drift in pendulum_lab or resonator_lab during Days 1–10, combined with a separate Day 23 acute disturbance: two independent problems producing the observed decorrelation and variance spike.

Measurement technique, observer identity, or protocol differences between 'lab' and 'observational' streams (different people, definitions of 'beat' or 'cycle', data reduction), combined with a Day 23 procedural change affecting lab observer or apparatus.
All four streams are independent noise with no underlying signal; observed correlations and Day 23 spike are statistical flukes or rare random excursions.
